blocks.text: Scenario A — History taking
A 35-year-old woman presents to the gynaecology clinic with irregular vaginal bleeding for six months. Take a focused history and outline your differential diagnoses.
Scenario B — Clinical assessment
A 42-year-old woman presents with prolonged, heavy menstrual bleeding and fatigue. Take a history, discuss your investigations and propose a management plan.
Scenario C — Emergency assessment
A 28-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Assess her and explain your immediate management.
Scenario D — Investigation interpretation
A 51-year-old woman presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Her ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium. Interpret the finding and explain the next steps.

Examiner's expectation: You should not immediately label every case as abnormal uterine bleeding. First assess haemodynamic stability, establish whether pregnancy is possible, characterise the bleeding and look for its cause.
Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is bleeding from the uterine corpus that is abnormal in volume, duration, regularity or frequency, in a non-pregnant patient of reproductive age.
It may be acute or chronic.

items.text: Acute AUB: bleeding severe enough to require immediate intervention to prevent further blood loss.
Chronic AUB: abnormal bleeding present for most of the preceding six months.
Intermenstrual bleeding: bleeding between otherwise recognisable menstrual periods.
Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB): menstrual blood loss that interferes with physical, social, emotional or material quality of life.

blocks.text: In a patient with vaginal bleeding, always consider pregnancy-related causes before applying the non-pregnant AUB classification.
This is one of the most important mnemonics to memorise for the examination.
P — Polyp
Endometrial or endocervical polyps can cause intermenstrual or irregular bleeding.
A — Adenomyosis
Endometrial tissue within the myometrium; classically associated with painful, heavy menstruation and a tender, bulky uterus.
L — Leiomyoma
Uterine fibroids, especially submucosal fibroids, can cause heavy or prolonged bleeding.
M — Malignancy and hyperplasia
Endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer must be considered, particularly with persistent bleeding, risk factors or postmenopausal bleeding.
C — Coagulopathy: von Willebrand disease, platelet disorders and other bleeding disorders.
O — Ovulatory dysfunction: PCOS, perimenopause, thyroid disorders and other causes of anovulation.
E — Endometrial: abnormalities of local endometrial haemostasis, often a diagnosis of exclusion.
I — Iatrogenic: hormonal contraception, anticoagulants and other medications.
N — Not otherwise classified: less common causes, such as uterine arteriovenous malformations.
Remember: more than one cause may coexist in the same patient.
Start every practical station professionally. These marks are often easy to obtain.

“Good morning. My name is …, and I am a medical doctor. I understand that you have been experiencing abnormal vaginal bleeding. I would like to ask you some questions about your periods, the bleeding and your general health so that I can understand what may be causing it. Some questions will be personal, but they will help me provide appropriate care. Is that okay?”

items.text: Confirm the patient's name and age.
Explain confidentiality and its limits where relevant.
Obtain consent to take the history.
Ask permission before discussing sexual or reproductive health.
Establish whether the patient is in pain or bleeding heavily at that moment.
If this is an examination station, explain the proposed examination and obtain separate consent.
Offer a chaperone for an intimate examination, according to local policy.
Maintain privacy, dignity and a non-judgmental attitude.

blocks.text: Important: If the patient appears unstable, do not spend several minutes completing a routine history before initiating emergency care.
Use a systematic approach. The goal is to identify the pattern of bleeding, assess its severity and discover the likely cause.

content_groups.group_title: A. Presenting complaint and history of presenting complaint

blocks.text: Begin with an open question:
“Can you tell me more about the bleeding you have been experiencing?”
Allow the patient to speak before asking focused questions.
**1. Onset and duration**

items.text: When did the bleeding first begin?
Was the onset sudden or gradual?
How long has this been happening?
Has it occurred before?
Is this the first episode or a recurrent problem?
Has the bleeding become progressively worse?

blocks.text: Interpretation

rows: Acute AUB; pregnancy-related bleeding must be excluded
Ovulatory dysfunction, including PCOS or perimenopause
Polyps, cervical disease or endometrial pathology

blocks.text: **2. Menstrual pattern**
Establish the patient's usual menstrual history and how it has changed.

items.text: At what age did your periods start?
When was the first day of your last menstrual period?
How many days are there between the starts of your periods?
Are your cycles regular or irregular?
How many days does bleeding usually last?
How long does it last now?
Have you missed periods before the bleeding started?

blocks.text: For an adult with regular cycles, a typical menstrual cycle frequency is approximately every 24–38 days, with bleeding lasting up to eight days. Individual patterns vary.

items.text: Frequent bleeding: cycles occurring more often than expected.
Infrequent bleeding: long intervals between periods.
Irregular bleeding: unpredictable cycle intervals.
Prolonged bleeding: bleeding lasting longer than expected.
Intermenstrual bleeding: bleeding between periods.
Postcoital bleeding: bleeding following sexual intercourse.

blocks.text: Do not assume that irregular bleeding automatically means PCOS. Pregnancy, thyroid disorders, perimenopause and other causes should also be considered.
**3. Amount of blood loss**
This is a critical part of the station.

items.text: How many sanitary pads or tampons do you use per day?
How often do you need to change them?
Do you soak through a pad within an hour?
Do you need to change pads during the night?
Do you need double protection?
Have you passed blood clots? How large are they?
Have you stained your clothes or bedsheets?
Does the bleeding interfere with work, sleep or normal activities?

blocks.text: Ask whether the patient uses menstrual cups or another method to estimate blood loss.
Abnormal findings and their significance

items.text: Repeatedly soaking a pad every hour may indicate substantial blood loss, especially when accompanied by dizziness or weakness.
Large clots can accompany heavy menstrual bleeding but do not establish its cause.
Bleeding that prevents the patient from performing normal daily activities is clinically significant, even if an exact blood volume cannot be measured.
Fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations and dizziness may indicate anaemia.

blocks.text: Do not rely solely on the number of pads used to estimate blood loss; absorbency, changing habits and product type vary.
**4. Associated symptoms**
Ask about the following:

rows: Pregnancy complications, ovarian pathology or other acute pelvic disease
Fibroids or an enlarged pelvic mass
Cervical ectropion, cervicitis, polyps or cervical malignancy
Weight gain, cold intolerance or constipation
Possible hyperprolactinaemia, especially with menstrual irregularity
Perimenopause or menopause, depending on context

blocks.text: Also ask about urinary and bowel symptoms, particularly if a pelvic mass or endometriosis is suspected.
Always consider pregnancy in a patient of reproductive potential, even if she reports irregular periods or uses contraception.

items.text: Is there any possibility that you could be pregnant?
When was your last normal period?
Are you sexually active?
What contraception do you use?
Have you missed any contraceptive pills or had contraceptive failure?
Have you recently had a miscarriage, abortion or delivery?
Have you previously had an ectopic pregnancy?

blocks.text: Bleeding accompanied by abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or marked dizziness requires urgent assessment for ectopic pregnancy and significant haemorrhage.

items.text: Previous fibroids, polyps or ovarian cysts.
Endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Previous pelvic inflammatory disease.
Previous cervical screening results.
Previous abnormal cervical cytology or HPV results.
Previous uterine surgery, curettage or caesarean section.
Previous endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy.
History of sexually transmitted infections.

blocks.text: Clarify any previous investigations and treatments, including their effectiveness.

blocks.title: Use the GTPAL framework where appropriate:

items.text: G — Gravidity: total number of pregnancies.
T — Term births: births at term.
P — Preterm births: births before term.
A — Abortions or pregnancy losses: according to the locally used definition.
L — Living children.

blocks.text: Ask about previous miscarriages, ectopic pregnancies, molar pregnancies, deliveries and postpartum haemorrhage.
Clarify that definitions of pregnancy loss and gestational thresholds can differ between clinical systems.

items.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills.
Progestogen-only pills.
Implants and injectable contraception.
Copper intrauterine devices.
Levonorgestrel intrauterine systems.
Hormone replacement therapy.
Tamoxifen.
Anticoagulants and antiplatelet medicines.
Other medicines associated with menstrual disturbance.

blocks.text: Establish when the medication was started and whether bleeding began after initiation or a change in dose.
For example, heavier periods may occur with a copper IUD, while irregular spotting can occur with progestogen-only contraception, especially after initiation.

items.text: Thyroid disease.
Diabetes and hypertension.
Liver or kidney disease.
Bleeding disorders.
Previous anaemia or blood transfusion.
Obesity and metabolic disorders.
Previous pelvic or abdominal surgery.
Personal history of endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy.
Endometrial, ovarian, breast or colorectal cancer.
Lynch syndrome or other hereditary cancer syndromes.
Bleeding disorders.
Similar menstrual problems in close relatives.

blocks.text: A family history of Lynch syndrome or related cancers may substantially alter the threshold for investigating endometrial pathology.
Approach these questions sensitively and explain their relevance.

items.text: Sexual activity and STI risk where relevant.
Smoking and alcohol use.
Weight changes, nutrition and exercise.
Psychosocial stress.
Impact on work, relationships and quality of life.
Whether the patient feels safe at home, if clinically indicated.

blocks.text: Do not assume that all patients are sexually active, married or seeking future pregnancy.

items.text: Would you like to have children in the future?
Have you completed your family?
Would you prefer to preserve your uterus?
How much is the bleeding affecting your daily life?
Have you tried any treatment?
What are your main concerns about the bleeding?

blocks.text: These questions directly influence the management plan. A treatment that is acceptable to a patient who has completed her family may not be appropriate for someone seeking pregnancy.
This is one of the most important decision points in the OSCE.
Emergency features

items.text: Hypotension, tachycardia or collapse.
Syncope, confusion or marked weakness.
Ongoing profuse bleeding.
Severe abdominal pain or peritonism.
Possible pregnancy with pain or haemodynamic compromise.

blocks.text: If stable
Complete the history, perform an appropriate examination, exclude pregnancy, assess for anaemia and investigate the likely cause.

If haemorrhage or ectopic pregnancy is suspected, initiate urgent assessment and treatment without waiting for all investigations. Obtain senior gynaecological support, establish IV access when indicated and assess the need for blood products and definitive intervention.
In an OSCE, explain what you would examine, obtain consent and offer a chaperone before any intimate examination.

items.text: General appearance and level of consciousness.
Pallor, suggesting anaemia.
Pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation as indicated.
Hydration and peripheral perfusion.
Body mass index where relevant.
Bruising or petechiae if a bleeding disorder is suspected.
Signs of thyroid disease or hyperandrogenism, such as hirsutism and acne.

blocks.text: In an acutely bleeding patient, repeat observations and assess haemodynamic stability.
Inspect for abdominal distension, scars and visible masses.

items.text: Suprapubic tenderness.
An enlarged uterus.
A pelvic or abdominal mass.
Guarding or rebound tenderness.
Organ enlargement, where indicated.

blocks.text: Examples of interpretation

rows: Pelvic infection or another inflammatory process
Acute abdominal or pelvic pathology requiring urgent assessment

blocks.text: These are suggestive findings, not definitive diagnoses.
Perform only when clinically indicated, with consent, privacy and an appropriate chaperone.
Speculum examination

blocks.title: Assess the vulva, vagina and cervix for:

items.text: The source and amount of bleeding.
Cervical ectropion or polyps.
Cervicitis or abnormal discharge.
Cervical lesions suspicious for malignancy.
Vaginal trauma or lesions.

blocks.text: Bimanual examination

items.text: Uterine size, shape, mobility and tenderness.
Cervical motion tenderness.
Adnexal tenderness or masses.
Pelvic fullness.

blocks.text: A pelvic examination may be inappropriate or need modification in some circumstances. In a severely unstable patient, do not delay resuscitation to complete it.

content_groups.group_title: D. How to report examination findings

blocks.text: Normal examination

“The patient is haemodynamically stable, with no obvious pallor. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no palpable masses. On pelvic examination, the cervix appears normal, with no obvious cervical lesion or active bleeding from a visible abnormality. The uterus is normal in size and non-tender, with no palpable adnexal mass.”
Example suggesting fibroids

“The patient is haemodynamically stable but appears pale. The abdomen reveals a firm, irregularly enlarged pelvic mass arising from the pelvis. Bimanual examination suggests an enlarged irregular uterus, consistent with possible uterine leiomyomas. I would confirm this with pelvic ultrasound and assess for anaemia.”
Example suggesting cervical pathology

“Speculum examination reveals a friable cervical lesion that bleeds on contact. This is suspicious for cervical pathology, including malignancy, and requires urgent specialist assessment, appropriate biopsy and staging investigations if cancer is confirmed.”
Never report a finding you have not actually observed.
A good candidate prioritises the differential diagnoses using the patient's age, bleeding pattern, symptoms and pregnancy status.

rows: Irregular periods in a young adult
Pregnancy, PCOS, thyroid dysfunction, ovulatory dysfunction
Heavy bleeding with an enlarged irregular uterus
Polyps, ovulatory dysfunction, cervical or endometrial pathology
Cervicitis, cervical ectropion, cervical polyp, cervical malignancy
Bleeding with pelvic pain and fever
PID, pregnancy complications, other acute pelvic pathology
Endometrial atrophy, polyps, endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, among other causes
Iatrogenic bleeding, while excluding other causes when indicated

content_groups.group_title: A special note on postmenopausal bleeding

blocks.text: Any bleeding after menopause warrants prompt assessment. Endometrial cancer must be excluded, even if the bleeding is light or occurs only once.
Do not reassure a patient solely because the bleeding has stopped.
Investigations should be tailored to the clinical presentation rather than ordered indiscriminately.
1. Full blood count (FBC)
Assesses haemoglobin and platelet count. Anaemia may result from prolonged or heavy bleeding.
2. Pregnancy test
Urine or serum β-hCG, as appropriate, in patients who could be pregnant. A positive result changes the diagnostic pathway.
3. Pelvic ultrasound

Transvaginal ultrasound is often preferred when appropriate and acceptable. Transabdominal ultrasound may complement it or be used instead. Assess the uterus, endometrium, fibroids, polyps and adnexa.
**Additional investigations**

rows: Suspected iron deficiency; NICE recommends considering it selectively rather than routinely in every patient with HMB
Suspected bleeding disorder, relevant medical history or anticoagulant-related concerns
Symptoms or signs of thyroid disease
Suspected hyperprolactinaemia, particularly with amenorrhoea or ovulatory dysfunction
Suspected cervicitis or PID, according to exposure and symptoms
According to screening eligibility, symptoms and examination findings
Suspected intracavitary pathology, such as a polyp or submucosal fibroid
Increased risk of endometrial pathology or persistent bleeding, according to the relevant guideline
Blood group, antibody screen and crossmatch
Significant active haemorrhage or anticipated transfusion
Relevant comorbidity, medication considerations or suspected systemic disease

blocks.text: **When is endometrial sampling indicated?**
Consider endometrial sampling when there is a meaningful risk of hyperplasia or malignancy. Examples include:

items.text: Persistent intermenstrual or irregular bleeding.
Persistent bleeding despite appropriate treatment.
Abnormal bleeding with risk factors for endometrial cancer.
Suspected endometrial pathology requiring histological diagnosis.

blocks.text: In US guidance, endometrial sampling is generally a first-line investigation for AUB in patients aged 45 years or older. UK pathways may use age, risk factors, symptoms and hysteroscopy findings to guide sampling rather than relying on a single age threshold.

For postmenopausal bleeding, transvaginal ultrasound and/or endometrial sampling may be appropriate depending on the presentation and local guideline. An endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less is reassuring in an initial episode of postmenopausal bleeding when the endometrium is adequately visualised, but persistent or recurrent bleeding still requires further assessment.

blocks.title: The management plan depends on four major factors:

items.text: Is the patient haemodynamically stable?
Is pregnancy present or possible?
What is the likely underlying cause?
Does the patient wish to preserve fertility?

content_groups.group_title: A. Acute heavy bleeding with haemodynamic instability

blocks.text: Treat this as an emergency.

items.text: Call for help. Involve senior gynaecology and anaesthesia teams as indicated.
Assess ABCDE. Monitor vital signs, mental status, perfusion and ongoing blood loss.
Establish IV access. Use appropriate large-bore access and obtain urgent blood tests, including FBC, blood group and crossmatch.
Resuscitate. Give appropriate IV fluids and blood products according to the clinical condition, haemorrhage severity and local major-haemorrhage protocol.
Exclude pregnancy-related emergencies. Perform urgent pregnancy testing and appropriate assessment for ectopic pregnancy or pregnancy loss.
Control the bleeding. Use appropriate medical or procedural treatment under specialist supervision, depending on the cause, contraindications and response.

blocks.text: Do not wait for the haemoglobin result before treating clinically significant haemorrhagic shock. Haemoglobin can initially underestimate acute blood loss.

content_groups.group_title: B. Stable patient with heavy menstrual bleeding

blocks.text: Treatment should be individualised. Discuss the benefits, adverse effects, contraindications, fertility plans and patient preferences.
1. Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS)
Often a first-line option for HMB when appropriate, particularly in the absence of significant cavity distortion or other contraindications. It can substantially reduce menstrual blood loss.
2. Tranexamic acid
A non-hormonal option taken during menstruation to reduce bleeding. Assess thrombotic history, contraindications and renal function where relevant.
3. Combined hormonal contraception
May regulate cycles and reduce bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. Assess eligibility, especially thromboembolic risk, migraine with aura, hypertension and smoking-related risk.
4. NSAIDs

Such as ibuprofen or naproxen, when suitable. They may reduce menstrual blood loss and relieve dysmenorrhoea. Avoid or use cautiously with renal impairment, peptic ulcer disease, relevant bleeding disorders and other contraindications.
5. Progestogen therapy
May be useful in selected patients, including some with anovulatory bleeding. The regimen depends on the cause and clinical circumstances.
Iron replacement should be offered when iron deficiency or iron-deficiency anaemia is established or strongly suspected, with follow-up to assess response.

content_groups.group_title: C. Management according to the cause

rows: Medical therapy, myomectomy, uterine artery embolisation or hysterectomy, depending on symptoms, anatomy and fertility plans
LNG-IUS, hormonal treatments, analgesia or surgery in selected cases
Endometrial protection with appropriate progestogen or hormonal contraception; address metabolic risk and fertility goals
Treat the bleeding disorder with haematology input where appropriate
Review the causative medicine and alternatives; do not stop essential anticoagulation without an appropriate clinical plan
Histology-directed treatment and surveillance, with specialist input
Urgent referral for diagnostic assessment, histology and appropriate staging

items.text: Medical treatment fails or is contraindicated.
A structural lesion requires treatment.
Bleeding is severe or recurrent.
There is significant anaemia or impairment of quality of life.
The patient prefers a procedural option after informed counselling.

blocks.text: Options include hysteroscopic treatment, selected endometrial ablation procedures, myomectomy and hysterectomy.

Fertility warning: Endometrial ablation is not appropriate for someone planning future pregnancy. Pregnancy after ablation can be dangerous, and effective contraception is required. Hysterectomy permanently ends the ability to carry a pregnancy.
A common OSCE task is to explain the diagnosis and proposed treatment in simple language.

“Abnormal uterine bleeding means that your periods are different from what would normally be expected in their timing, duration or amount. There are several possible causes, including hormonal changes, fibroids, polyps and problems with the lining of the womb.

First, we need to assess how much blood you have lost and check whether you have developed anaemia. Depending on your symptoms, we may recommend a pregnancy test, blood tests and an ultrasound scan. If there are concerns about the lining of the womb, further assessment or a biopsy may be necessary.

There are several treatment options. Some medicines reduce bleeding, while hormonal treatments can regulate periods. If a fibroid or polyp is responsible, a procedure may be more suitable. The best option will depend on the cause, your general health and whether you wish to have children in the future.
If you experience very heavy ongoing bleeding, fainting, severe abdominal pain, breathlessness at rest or marked dizziness, please seek urgent medical attention.”
Finish by asking:
“Do you have any questions or concerns about the investigations or treatment we have discussed?”

content_groups.group_title: Question 1: What is abnormal uterine bleeding?

blocks.text: Bleeding from the uterine corpus that is abnormal in frequency, regularity, duration or volume in a non-pregnant patient of reproductive age.

It is the FIGO classification of causes of AUB. PALM represents structural causes: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, and malignancy/hyperplasia. COEIN represents coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial causes, iatrogenic causes and causes not otherwise classified.

content_groups.group_title: Question 3: What is your first investigation in a reproductive-age patient?

blocks.text: A pregnancy test should be performed whenever pregnancy is possible. FBC is also important in heavy or prolonged bleeding to assess anaemia and platelet count.

content_groups.group_title: Question 4: What are the red flags?

blocks.text: Haemodynamic instability, ongoing profuse bleeding, syncope, severe abdominal pain, possible ectopic pregnancy, postmenopausal bleeding and persistent bleeding with risk factors for malignancy.

content_groups.group_title: Question 5: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

blocks.text: Pelvic ultrasound, often transvaginal ultrasound when appropriate. Hysteroscopy may be needed when intracavitary pathology is suspected.

content_groups.group_title: Question 6: When would you perform an endometrial biopsy?

blocks.text: When age, risk factors, persistent symptoms or clinical findings suggest endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy. The exact pathway depends on the guideline and presentation.

content_groups.group_title: Question 7: What is the first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding?

blocks.text: The LNG-IUS is a common first-line option when suitable, particularly when there is no significant cavity distortion or relevant contraindication. Tranexamic acid, NSAIDs and hormonal alternatives are options depending on the patient's circumstances.

content_groups.group_title: Question 8: Why is fertility preference important?

blocks.text: Because hormonal treatment, myomectomy, ablation and hysterectomy have different implications for future pregnancy. Ablation and hysterectomy are incompatible with plans to carry a future pregnancy.

content_groups.group_title: Question 9: How would you manage severe acute AUB?

blocks.text: ABCDE assessment, urgent senior help, IV access, appropriate blood tests and crossmatch, resuscitation when indicated, exclusion of pregnancy-related emergencies and prompt bleeding control.

content_groups.group_title: Question 10: What is the difference between AUB and HMB?

blocks.text: AUB is the broader term covering abnormalities in bleeding frequency, regularity, duration or volume. HMB specifically refers to menstrual blood loss that adversely affects the patient's quality of life.

items.text: Forgetting to exclude pregnancy.
Failing to assess haemodynamic stability before taking a lengthy history.
Asking how many pads are used but not asking how quickly they become soaked.
Failing to ask about intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Ignoring postmenopausal bleeding.
Ordering thyroid tests routinely without relevant clinical indications.
Forgetting medication-related bleeding and anticoagulant use.
Assuming all irregular bleeding is due to PCOS.
Recommending a treatment without considering contraindications or fertility preferences.
Performing an intimate examination without appropriate consent and a chaperone.
Reassuring a patient with persistent symptoms solely because an initial ultrasound is reassuring.

blocks.text: B — Bleeding pattern, burden and duration.
L — Last menstrual period and likelihood of pregnancy.
E — Extra symptoms: pain, fever, fatigue and postcoital bleeding.
E — Existing gynaecological disease, medication and endocrine history.
D — Desires for future fertility and impact on daily life.
Remember this classification exactly; it is a frequent examiner question.
S — Stability and severity.
T — Test for pregnancy.
A — Assess anaemia and blood loss.
B — Bleeding pattern and associated symptoms.
L — Look for structural and other causes.
E — Establish an individualised treatment plan.
If the examiner asks you to summarise your assessment, use this structure:

“This is a [age]-year-old woman presenting with [duration] of [heavy, prolonged, irregular or intermenstrual] uterine bleeding. She is currently [haemodynamically stable/unstable]. The bleeding is associated with [relevant symptoms], and her pregnancy status is [known/awaiting testing].

My differential diagnoses include [most likely cause], [second possibility] and [important diagnosis that must be excluded]. I would assess her vital signs, perform a focused abdominal and indicated pelvic examination, obtain a pregnancy test where appropriate, request a full blood count and arrange pelvic imaging. Further testing, including endometrial assessment, would depend on her age, risk factors and clinical findings.

Management would be guided by the severity of bleeding, the underlying cause, contraindications and her fertility preferences. If unstable, I would initiate emergency resuscitation and urgent specialist management.”
1. A 29-year-old woman has irregular periods, obesity and hirsutism. Which PALM–COEIN category is most relevant?
Polyp
Ovulatory dysfunction
Coagulopathy
Iatrogenic
2. A 47-year-old woman has persistent intermenstrual bleeding. What is an important next step?
Reassure without investigation
Prescribe iron only
Investigate for endometrial pathology based on risk and findings
Assume it is menopause
3. A woman with heavy vaginal bleeding is faint and hypotensive. What is your priority?
Arrange an outpatient ultrasound
Complete the full menstrual history
Initiate emergency ABCDE assessment and resuscitation
Book routine follow-up
